title: How Mexican Wrestling Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Mexican wrestling (lucha libre), tracing its origins from American carnival wrestling and the gold Dust Trio, through Don Salvador Lutteroth Gonzalez founding the EMLL after the Spanish Civil War, to the luchador culture of masks, technicos and rudos, lucha de apuestas (masked wagers), weight classes, match rules, tag and trios matches, signature moves like the plancha, tope and hurricanrana, and key figures such as El Santo, Blue Demon, Mysterio, and Cassandro. They also cover rival leagues (AAA, CMLL), Chikara, Lucha VaVoom, openly gay exotico wrestlers, and the masked crusader Super Barrio. The episode ends with a request for iTunes ratings and listener mail call for submissions.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Mexican wrestling
segments.summary: Hosts banter about names and Chuck's luchador name, then introduce Mexican wrestling (lucha libre) as a fun topic and mention an upcoming pro wrestling documentary and Andre the Giant references.

segments.title: Origins: American carnival wrestling and the gold Dust Trio
segments.summary: Professional wrestling began in late nineteenth century America and became staged in the 1920s under the gold Dust Trio, who embraced carnival-style entertainment and kayfabe. The hosts discuss the fake storylines versus real athleticism.

segments.title: Founding of Mexican wrestling and the EMLL
segments.summary: Don Salvador Lutteroth Gonzalez founded the first Mexican wrestling league, the EMLL, after wrestling came from Spain (catch) and migrated to Mexico during the Spanish Civil War; the Texas carnival wrestling scene is cited as inspiration.

segments.title: Lucha libre culture: luchadors, masks and identity
segments.summary: Chuck translates lucha libre as free fighting and explains the luchador identity, the importance of masks, and how wrestlers carry their personas outside the ring and pass them to sons.

segments.title: Technicos, rudos and populist storylines
segments.summary: Good guys (technicos) are populist heroes like superheroes or saints who fight for the poor, while bad guys (rudos) play corrupt cops, officials, or gangsters. The hosts note good typically wins, though good villains are also popular.

segments.title: Lucha de apuestas: masked and hair wager matches
segments.summary: Lucha de apuestas matches are wagers of masks, hair, or careers; the loser is unmasked or must retire and reveal their name and hometown. The hosts debate whether losers can keep wrestling masked and note the matches are rare.

segments.title: Style, weight classes and match rules
segments.summary: Luchadors are often smaller and faster with high-flying acrobatics. Weight classes derive from boxing, with the welterweight joke. Single matches end by pin, count-out, submission, or disqualification; weapons, groin shots, and attacking referees are banned; mercy rule is referee stoppage for excessive punishment.

segments.title: Tag team and trios matches and signature moves
segments.summary: Trios matches are most popular, with rules to pin the captain or both others; tag rules differ from American wrestling since partners can enter after someone leaves the ring. Moves described include the plancha, tornillo, senton, tope, leg twist, and hurricanrana.

segments.title: El Santo, Blue Demon, and luchadors as national icons
segments.summary: Luchadors are national icons in Mexico. El Santo was a technico who appeared in comics (fotonovelas), around fifty two movies, and was never publicly unmasked until he unmasked on TV shortly before death; both he and Blue Demon were buried in masks. Blue Demon was an early aerial specialist and crossover star.

segments.title: Crossover to US, women, minis, exotico and Super Barrio
segments.summary: Rey Mysterio and Mystico crossed to WWE, with Mystico renamed Sin Cara. The hosts discuss women luchadoras, minis (little people and small wrestlers), openly gay exotico wrestlers such as Udra, Cassandro, and the masked activist Super Barrio.

segments.title: Wrap-up, promotion and listener mail call
segments.summary: Hosts mention Nacho Libre, ask for iTunes ratings, promote their video podcast, and invite listener mail. No listener mail is read this episode.
